02f8f0aee316.reason: PostTeam() inserts into teams and then reads the generated id back with LastInsertId() on the same connection. LAST_INSERT_ID() is connection-scoped session state, so the read is only correct while it shares a connection with the write. Converting this would move the id onto GORM map-Create's undocumented "@id" writeback and hand the connection choice to the dbresolver plugin. The failure mode is not an error: it is a row created against the wrong parent id, found days later. Enforced by ratchet gate (k); see tools/orm-migration/lastinsertid-sites.json.
02f8f0aee316.porting: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... RETURNING id. This is the one category that gets EASIER on Postgres - RETURNING is part of the statement, so the id comes back with the insert and the connection-scoped LAST_INSERT_ID() problem disappears entirely. GORM exposes it via clause.Returning, so these sites may become convertible during the port rather than staying raw.

049bc3f964cd.reason: REPLACE INTO cannot be expressed via GORM's clause.Insert. The framework writes the clause's Name() ("INSERT") before calling Build(), and Insert.Build() only ever appends a Modifier word plus "INTO" after that literal "INSERT" - so Modifier:"REPLACE" would render "INSERT REPLACE INTO ...", not "REPLACE INTO ...". There is no clause that swaps the statement keyword itself, unlike INSERT IGNORE (wave 3's clause.Insert{Modifier:"IGNORE"}) which only ever needed a modifier, not a different keyword.
049bc3f964cd.porting: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (cols) DO UPDATE. Note this is NOT a behavioural equivalent. MySQL REPLACE deletes the conflicting row and inserts a new one, which fires DELETE triggers, cascades foreign keys, and assigns a NEW auto-increment id. ON CONFLICT updates in place, keeping the row and its id. Anything depending on the row identity changing, or on ON DELETE CASCADE firing, changes behaviour at the port.

050e3574aa6f.goldenSql: INSERT INTO chat_rooms (user1, user2, chattype, latestmessage) VALUES (?, ?, ?, NOW()) ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE id = LAST_INSERT_ID(id), latestmessage = NOW()
050e3574aa6f.reason: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE id = LAST_INSERT_ID(id), whose generated id the caller reads back. Note what this is NOT: it is not a cross-statement dependency on session state. LAST_INSERT_ID(expr) is the one-argument form, which makes the server report expr in the OK packet for THAT statement, so sql.Result.LastInsertId() reads it exactly as for a plain insert. The idiom exists so a conflicting upsert returns the EXISTING row id rather than nothing. It renders fine under GORM - clause.OnConflict with an ordered clause.Set carrying gorm.Expr("LAST_INSERT_ID(id)") - and inserting, or colliding and changing a column, both return the right id (measured in test/orm_upsert_id_test.go). What blocks a mechanical conversion is narrower and real: GORM returns early from its create callback when RowsAffected is 0 (callbacks/create.go:123) and skips the id writeback, and MySQL reports 0 rows affected for an upsert that matched but changed nothing. So a repeat upsert with identical values leaves "@id" absent where the raw code still got the id back. Converting means handling a missing id with a lookup at each call site, which is a behaviour change to review rather than a swap - a deliberate decision, not an impossibility.
050e3574aa6f.porting: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (cols) DO UPDATE SET ... RETURNING id, which is strictly better - RETURNING reports the id on both the insert and the conflict path, so the rowsAffected=0 gap that blocks the MySQL/GORM conversion does not exist. These become ordinary at the port. Note ON CONFLICT needs a named unique index or constraint on the conflict target, which Postgres will not infer.
050e3574aa6f.category: ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE id = LAST_INSERT_ID(id)

09730933af57.reason: REPLACE INTO cannot be expressed via GORM's clause.Insert. The framework writes the clause's Name() ("INSERT") before calling Build(), and Insert.Build() only ever appends a Modifier word plus "INTO" after that literal "INSERT" (confirmed by rendering gorm.io/gorm/clause's own insert_test.go cases: Modifier:"LOW_PRIORITY" renders "INSERT LOW_PRIORITY INTO ...") - so Modifier:"REPLACE" would render "INSERT REPLACE INTO ...", not "REPLACE INTO ...". There is no clause that swaps the statement keyword itself, unlike INSERT IGNORE (wave 3's clause.Insert{Modifier:"IGNORE"}) which only ever needed a modifier, not a different keyword.
09730933af57.porting: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (cols) DO UPDATE. Note this is NOT a behavioural equivalent. MySQL REPLACE deletes the conflicting row and inserts a new one, which fires DELETE triggers, cascades foreign keys, and assigns a NEW auto-increment id. ON CONFLICT updates in place, keeping the row and its id. Anything depending on the row identity changing, or on ON DELETE CASCADE firing, changes behaviour at the port.

0adadbabde5b.reason: Create() inserts into volunteering and then reads the generated id back with LastInsertId() on the same connection. LAST_INSERT_ID() is connection-scoped session state, so the read is only correct while it shares a connection with the write. Converting this would move the id onto GORM map-Create's undocumented "@id" writeback and hand the connection choice to the dbresolver plugin. The failure mode is not an error: it is a row created against the wrong parent id, found days later. Enforced by ratchet gate (k); see tools/orm-migration/lastinsertid-sites.json.
0adadbabde5b.porting: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... RETURNING id. This is the one category that gets EASIER on Postgres - RETURNING is part of the statement, so the id comes back with the insert and the connection-scoped LAST_INSERT_ID() problem disappears entirely. GORM exposes it via clause.Returning, so these sites may become convertible during the port rather than staying raw.

123512413259.reason: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE id = LAST_INSERT_ID(id), whose generated id the caller reads back. Note what this is NOT: it is not a cross-statement dependency on session state. LAST_INSERT_ID(expr) is the one-argument form, which makes the server report expr in the OK packet for THAT statement, so sql.Result.LastInsertId() reads it exactly as for a plain insert. The idiom exists so a conflicting upsert returns the EXISTING row id rather than nothing. It renders fine under GORM - clause.OnConflict with an ordered clause.Set carrying gorm.Expr("LAST_INSERT_ID(id)") - and inserting, or colliding and changing a column, both return the right id (measured in test/orm_upsert_id_test.go). What blocks a mechanical conversion is narrower and real: GORM returns early from its create callback when RowsAffected is 0 (callbacks/create.go:123) and skips the id writeback, and MySQL reports 0 rows affected for an upsert that matched but changed nothing. So a repeat upsert with identical values leaves "@id" absent where the raw code still got the id back. Converting means handling a missing id with a lookup at each call site, which is a behaviour change to review rather than a swap - a deliberate decision, not an impossibility.
123512413259.porting: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (cols) DO UPDATE SET ... RETURNING id, which is strictly better - RETURNING reports the id on both the insert and the conflict path, so the rowsAffected=0 gap that blocks the MySQL/GORM conversion does not exist. These become ordinary at the port. Note ON CONFLICT needs a named unique index or constraint on the conflict target, which Postgres will not infer.

1ff179ae0e2c.reason: REPLACE INTO cannot be expressed via GORM's clause.Insert. The framework writes the clause's Name() ("INSERT") before calling Build(), and Insert.Build() only ever appends a Modifier word plus "INTO" after that literal "INSERT" (confirmed by rendering gorm.io/gorm/clause's own insert_test.go cases: Modifier:"LOW_PRIORITY" renders "INSERT LOW_PRIORITY INTO ...") - so Modifier:"REPLACE" would render "INSERT REPLACE INTO ...", not "REPLACE INTO ...". There is no clause that swaps the statement keyword itself, unlike INSERT IGNORE (wave 3's clause.Insert{Modifier:"IGNORE"}) which only ever needed a modifier, not a different keyword.
1ff179ae0e2c.porting: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (cols) DO UPDATE. Note this is NOT a behavioural equivalent. MySQL REPLACE deletes the conflicting row and inserts a new one, which fires DELETE triggers, cascades foreign keys, and assigns a NEW auto-increment id. ON CONFLICT updates in place, keeping the row and its id. Anything depending on the row identity changing, or on ON DELETE CASCADE firing, changes behaviour at the port.

1ff296c8656c.reason: Runtime-varying: the statement has more than one possible rendered form (the statement is baseQuery+widerQuery, both built from recipientExpr (a CASE expression assembled elsewhere in the function) and a literal-value group-id list, neither of which is a fixed constant), captured by the extractor as an unresolved "{{expr}}"/"%d" placeholder in the recorded goldenSql rather than as a bind parameter. Worth reviewing these for whether the dynamic assembly is still needed at all, since several build a WHERE from a fixed set of options that a query builder could express directly.

258437a60f5d.reason: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE id = LAST_INSERT_ID(id), whose generated id the caller reads back. Note what this is NOT: it is not a cross-statement dependency on session state. LAST_INSERT_ID(expr) is the one-argument form, which makes the server report expr in the OK packet for THAT statement, so sql.Result.LastInsertId() reads it exactly as for a plain insert. The idiom exists so a conflicting upsert returns the EXISTING row id rather than nothing. It renders fine under GORM - clause.OnConflict with an ordered clause.Set carrying gorm.Expr("LAST_INSERT_ID(id)") - and inserting, or colliding and changing a column, both return the right id (measured in test/orm_upsert_id_test.go). What blocks a mechanical conversion is narrower and real: GORM returns early from its create callback when RowsAffected is 0 (callbacks/create.go:123) and skips the id writeback, and MySQL reports 0 rows affected for an upsert that matched but changed nothing. So a repeat upsert with identical values leaves "@id" absent where the raw code still got the id back. Converting means handling a missing id with a lookup at each call site, which is a behaviour change to review rather than a swap - a deliberate decision, not an impossibility.
258437a60f5d.porting: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (cols) DO UPDATE SET ... RETURNING id, which is strictly better - RETURNING reports the id on both the insert and the conflict path, so the rowsAffected=0 gap that blocks the MySQL/GORM conversion does not exist. These become ordinary at the port. Note ON CONFLICT needs a named unique index or constraint on the conflict target, which Postgres will not infer.
258437a60f5d.category: ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE id = LAST_INSERT_ID(id)

3c0db7c93a36.reason: INSERT whose caller needs LastInsertId. These sites use sqlDB.Exec deliberately so the id is read from the MySQL protocol response on the very connection that performed the insert. The hazard being avoided is NOT replication lag: LAST_INSERT_ID() is connection-scoped session state, so a follow-up SELECT can be handed a different pooled connection and return 0 or another session's id, as the comment in session/social_auth.go already spells out. Converting to GORM's Create would instead depend on primary-key writeback that, traced through callbacks/create.go in v1.31.0, stores the id under the literal key "@id" when stmt.Schema is nil - real behaviour, but undocumented, contradicted by the public docs, and untested upstream. Relying on that for the one value these sites exist to protect is precisely the silent, expensive rewrite bug plan 7.5 reserves keep-raw for. database/insert.go's ExecInsertGetID already encapsulates this pattern and is itself recorded as non-migration infrastructure; pointing these call sites at it would be a sensible dedup, but that is a refactor rather than an ORM conversion.
3c0db7c93a36.porting: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... RETURNING id. This is the one category that gets EASIER on Postgres - RETURNING is part of the statement, so the id comes back with the insert and the connection-scoped LAST_INSERT_ID() problem disappears entirely. GORM exposes it via clause.Returning, so these sites may become convertible during the port rather than staying raw.

3efeb225c001.reason: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE id = LAST_INSERT_ID(id), whose generated id the caller reads back. Note what this is NOT: it is not a cross-statement dependency on session state. LAST_INSERT_ID(expr) is the one-argument form, which makes the server report expr in the OK packet for THAT statement, so sql.Result.LastInsertId() reads it exactly as for a plain insert. The idiom exists so a conflicting upsert returns the EXISTING row id rather than nothing. It renders fine under GORM - clause.OnConflict with an ordered clause.Set carrying gorm.Expr("LAST_INSERT_ID(id)") - and inserting, or colliding and changing a column, both return the right id (measured in test/orm_upsert_id_test.go). What blocks a mechanical conversion is narrower and real: GORM returns early from its create callback when RowsAffected is 0 (callbacks/create.go:123) and skips the id writeback, and MySQL reports 0 rows affected for an upsert that matched but changed nothing. So a repeat upsert with identical values leaves "@id" absent where the raw code still got the id back. Converting means handling a missing id with a lookup at each call site, which is a behaviour change to review rather than a swap - a deliberate decision, not an impossibility.
3efeb225c001.porting: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (cols) DO UPDATE SET ... RETURNING id, which is strictly better - RETURNING reports the id on both the insert and the conflict path, so the rowsAffected=0 gap that blocks the MySQL/GORM conversion does not exist. These become ordinary at the port. Note ON CONFLICT needs a named unique index or constraint on the conflict target, which Postgres will not infer.

4aef5392a01f.reason: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE id = LAST_INSERT_ID(id), whose generated id the caller reads back. Note what this is NOT: it is not a cross-statement dependency on session state. LAST_INSERT_ID(expr) is the one-argument form, which makes the server report expr in the OK packet for THAT statement, so sql.Result.LastInsertId() reads it exactly as for a plain insert. The idiom exists so a conflicting upsert returns the EXISTING row id rather than nothing. It renders fine under GORM - clause.OnConflict with an ordered clause.Set carrying gorm.Expr("LAST_INSERT_ID(id)") - and inserting, or colliding and changing a column, both return the right id (measured in test/orm_upsert_id_test.go). What blocks a mechanical conversion is narrower and real: GORM returns early from its create callback when RowsAffected is 0 (callbacks/create.go:123) and skips the id writeback, and MySQL reports 0 rows affected for an upsert that matched but changed nothing. So a repeat upsert with identical values leaves "@id" absent where the raw code still got the id back. Converting means handling a missing id with a lookup at each call site, which is a behaviour change to review rather than a swap - a deliberate decision, not an impossibility.
4aef5392a01f.porting: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (cols) DO UPDATE SET ... RETURNING id, which is strictly better - RETURNING reports the id on both the insert and the conflict path, so the rowsAffected=0 gap that blocks the MySQL/GORM conversion does not exist. These become ordinary at the port. Note ON CONFLICT needs a named unique index or constraint on the conflict target, which Postgres will not infer.

These sites use sqlDB.Exec deliberately so the id is read from the MySQL protocol response on the very connection that performed the insert. The hazard being avoided is NOT replication lag: LAST_INSERT_ID() is connection-scoped session state, so a follow-up SELECT can be handed a different pooled connection and return 0 or another session's id, as the comment in session/social_auth.go already spells out. Converting to GORM's Create would instead depend on primary-key writeback that, traced through callbacks/create.go in v1.31.0, stores the id under the literal key "@id" when stmt.Schema is nil - real behaviour, but undocumented, contradicted by the public docs, and untested upstream. Relying on that for the one value these sites exist to protect is precisely the silent, expensive rewrite bug plan 7.5 reserves keep-raw for. database/insert.go's ExecInsertGetID already encapsulates this pattern and is itself recorded as non-migration infrastructure; pointing these call sites at it would be a sensible dedup, but that is a refactor rather than an ORM conversion.

This is the one category that gets EASIER on Postgres - RETURNING is part of the statement, so the id comes back with the insert and the connection-scoped LAST_INSERT_ID() problem disappears entirely. 65574169749a.reason: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE id = LAST_INSERT_ID(id), whose generated id the caller reads back. Note what this is NOT: it is not a cross-statement dependency on session state. LAST_INSERT_ID(expr) is the one-argument form, which makes the server report expr in the OK packet for THAT statement, so sql.Result.LastInsertId() reads it exactly as for a plain insert. The idiom exists so a conflicting upsert returns the EXISTING row id rather than nothing. It renders fine under GORM - clause.OnConflict with an ordered clause.Set carrying gorm.Expr("LAST_INSERT_ID(id)") - and inserting, or colliding and changing a column, both return the right id (measured in test/orm_upsert_id_test.go). What blocks a mechanical conversion is narrower and real: GORM returns early from its create callback when RowsAffected is 0 (callbacks/create.go:123) and skips the id writeback, and MySQL reports 0 rows affected for an upsert that matched but changed nothing. So a repeat upsert with identical values leaves "@id" absent where the raw code still got the id back. Converting means handling a missing id with a lookup at each call site, which is a behaviour change to review rather than a swap - a deliberate decision, not an impossibility.
65574169749a.porting: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (cols) DO UPDATE SET ... RETURNING id, which is strictly better - RETURNING reports the id on both the insert and the conflict path, so the rowsAffected=0 gap that blocks the MySQL/GORM conversion does not exist. These become ordinary at the port. Note ON CONFLICT needs a named unique index or constraint on the conflict target, which Postgres will not infer.
65574169749a.category: ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE id = LAST_INSERT_ID(id)

67871ee12b8f.reason: REPLACE INTO cannot be expressed via GORM's clause.Insert. The framework writes the clause's Name() ("INSERT") before calling Build(), and Insert.Build() only ever appends a Modifier word plus "INTO" after that literal "INSERT" - so Modifier:"REPLACE" would render "INSERT REPLACE INTO ...", not "REPLACE INTO ...". There is no clause that swaps the statement keyword itself, unlike INSERT IGNORE (wave 3's clause.Insert{Modifier:"IGNORE"}) which only ever needed a modifier, not a different keyword.
67871ee12b8f.porting: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (cols) DO UPDATE. Note this is NOT a behavioural equivalent. MySQL REPLACE deletes the conflicting row and inserts a new one, which fires DELETE triggers, cascades foreign keys, and assigns a NEW auto-increment id. ON CONFLICT updates in place, keeping the row and its id. Anything depending on the row identity changing, or on ON DELETE CASCADE firing, changes behaviour at the port.

6f1d6543e5c0.reason: REPLACE INTO cannot be expressed via GORM's clause.Insert. The framework writes the clause's Name() ("INSERT") before calling Build(), and Insert.Build() only ever appends a Modifier word plus "INTO" after that literal "INSERT" - so Modifier:"REPLACE" would render "INSERT REPLACE INTO ...", not "REPLACE INTO ...". There is no clause that swaps the statement keyword itself, unlike INSERT IGNORE (wave 3's clause.Insert{Modifier:"IGNORE"}) which only ever needed a modifier, not a different keyword. Also carries a second, independent blocker: the SRID is embedded via fmt.Sprintf(..., utils.SRID) as a literal %d BEFORE the string ever reaches Exec, so the manifest's recorded goldenSql is unresolved template text ("ST_GeomFromText(?, %d)") rather than real SQL - there is nothing for a rendered statement to compare against even setting the REPLACE issue aside.
6f1d6543e5c0.porting: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (cols) DO UPDATE. Note this is NOT a behavioural equivalent. MySQL REPLACE deletes the conflicting row and inserts a new one, which fires DELETE triggers, cascades foreign keys, and assigns a NEW auto-increment id. ON CONFLICT updates in place, keeping the row and its id. Anything depending on the row identity changing, or on ON DELETE CASCADE firing, changes behaviour at the port.

7e3e5f4d0b36.reason: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE id = LAST_INSERT_ID(id), whose generated id the caller reads back. Note what this is NOT: it is not a cross-statement dependency on session state. LAST_INSERT_ID(expr) is the one-argument form, which makes the server report expr in the OK packet for THAT statement, so sql.Result.LastInsertId() reads it exactly as for a plain insert. The idiom exists so a conflicting upsert returns the EXISTING row id rather than nothing. It renders fine under GORM - clause.OnConflict with an ordered clause.Set carrying gorm.Expr("LAST_INSERT_ID(id)") - and inserting, or colliding and changing a column, both return the right id (measured in test/orm_upsert_id_test.go). What blocks a mechanical conversion is narrower and real: GORM returns early from its create callback when RowsAffected is 0 (callbacks/create.go:123) and skips the id writeback, and MySQL reports 0 rows affected for an upsert that matched but changed nothing. So a repeat upsert with identical values leaves "@id" absent where the raw code still got the id back. Converting means handling a missing id with a lookup at each call site, which is a behaviour change to review rather than a swap - a deliberate decision, not an impossibility.
7e3e5f4d0b36.porting: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (cols) DO UPDATE SET ... RETURNING id, which is strictly better - RETURNING reports the id on both the insert and the conflict path, so the rowsAffected=0 gap that blocks the MySQL/GORM conversion does not exist. These become ordinary at the port. Note ON CONFLICT needs a named unique index or constraint on the conflict target, which Postgres will not infer.

7efd04588fb2.porting: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (cols) DO UPDATE. Note this is NOT a behavioural equivalent. MySQL REPLACE deletes the conflicting row and inserts a new one, which fires DELETE triggers, cascades foreign keys, and assigns a NEW auto-increment id. ON CONFLICT updates in place, keeping the row and its id. Anything depending on the row identity changing, or on ON DELETE CASCADE firing, changes behaviour at the port.

c1fca2fe89a0.reason: INSERT whose caller needs LastInsertId. These sites use sqlDB.Exec deliberately so the id is read from the MySQL protocol response on the very connection that performed the insert. The hazard being avoided is NOT replication lag: LAST_INSERT_ID() is connection-scoped session state, so a follow-up SELECT can be handed a different pooled connection and return 0 or another session's id, as the comment in session/social_auth.go already spells out. Converting to GORM's Create would instead depend on primary-key writeback that, traced through callbacks/create.go in v1.31.0, stores the id under the literal key "@id" when stmt.Schema is nil - real behaviour, but undocumented, contradicted by the public docs, and untested upstream. Relying on that for the one value these sites exist to protect is precisely the silent, expensive rewrite bug plan 7.5 reserves keep-raw for. database/insert.go's ExecInsertGetID already encapsulates this pattern and is itself recorded as non-migration infrastructure; pointing these call sites at it would be a sensible dedup, but that is a refactor rather than an ORM conversion.
c1fca2fe89a0.porting: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... RETURNING id. This is the one category that gets EASIER on Postgres - RETURNING is part of the statement, so the id comes back with the insert and the connection-scoped LAST_INSERT_ID() problem disappears entirely. GORM exposes it via clause.Returning, so these sites may become convertible during the port rather than staying raw.

The framework writes the clause's Name() ("INSERT") before calling Build(), and Insert.Build() only ever appends a Modifier word plus "INTO" after that literal "INSERT" - so Modifier:"REPLACE" would render "INSERT REPLACE INTO ...", not "REPLACE INTO ...". dfc3d2fdb2ba.reason: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE id = LAST_INSERT_ID(id), whose generated id the caller reads back. Note what this is NOT: it is not a cross-statement dependency on session state. LAST_INSERT_ID(expr) is the one-argument form, which makes the server report expr in the OK packet for THAT statement, so sql.Result.LastInsertId() reads it exactly as for a plain insert. The idiom exists so a conflicting upsert returns the EXISTING row id rather than nothing. It renders fine under GORM - clause.OnConflict with an ordered clause.Set carrying gorm.Expr("LAST_INSERT_ID(id)") - and inserting, or colliding and changing a column, both return the right id (measured in test/orm_upsert_id_test.go). What blocks a mechanical conversion is narrower and real: GORM returns early from its create callback when RowsAffected is 0 (callbacks/create.go:123) and skips the id writeback, and MySQL reports 0 rows affected for an upsert that matched but changed nothing. So a repeat upsert with identical values leaves "@id" absent where the raw code still got the id back. f3a8b6237a60.reason: REPLACE INTO cannot be expressed via GORM's clause.Insert. The framework writes the clause's Name() ("INSERT") before calling Build(), and Insert.Build() only ever appends a Modifier word plus "INTO" after that literal "INSERT" (confirmed by rendering gorm.io/gorm/clause's own insert_test.go cases: Modifier:"LOW_PRIORITY" renders "INSERT LOW_PRIORITY INTO ...") - so Modifier:"REPLACE" would render "INSERT REPLACE INTO ...", not "REPLACE INTO ...". There is no clause that swaps the statement keyword itself, unlike INSERT IGNORE (wave 3's clause.Insert{Modifier:"IGNORE"}) which only ever needed a modifier, not a different keyword.
f3a8b6237a60.porting: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (cols) DO UPDATE. Note this is NOT a behavioural equivalent. MySQL REPLACE deletes the conflicting row and inserts a new one, which fires DELETE triggers, cascades foreign keys, and assigns a NEW auto-increment id. ON CONFLICT updates in place, keeping the row and its id. Anything depending on the row identity changing, or on ON DELETE CASCADE firing, changes behaviour at the port.
